title: Maryland allows new chicken house construction to resume after permitting delay
summary: For more than nine months, Maryland poultry farmers haven't been able to build any new chicken houses because the state had not issued a pollution permit setting environmental requirements for animal feeding operations. That wait came to an end Friday.
content:
by Christine Condon, Maryland Matters April 24, 2026

by Christine Condon, Maryland Matters April 24, 2026

For more than nine months, poultry farmers in Maryland weren’t allowed to build any new chicken houses, as they awaited a delayed permit from the state’s environmental agency.

Their wait ended Friday, when the Maryland Department of the Environment issued the pollution permit that sets environmental requirements for animal feeding operations across the state. It replaces a previous permit covering the industry, which expired in July, causing the construction holdup.

The new permit is scheduled to take effect May 8, though anyone concerned about the permit’s provisions can file a judicial challenge until June 8, according to the agency’s website.

It comes after Maryland lawmakers got involved during the recently concluded legislative session, passing an emergency bill that would have allowed chicken house construction under certain circumstances after a permit’s expiration.

But Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) has yet to sign the bill, so it hasn’t taken effect — meaning MDE was able to fix its problem before legislators could.

Moore signs legislation in batches, and the bill on chicken houses was not included in his first batch earlier this month. A spokesman for the governor declined to comment on which bills will be included on Tuesday, his next scheduled bill-signing day.

Though the bill ultimately passed both chambers of the legislature unanimously, it was controversial at first. Environmentalists warned that the bill was too broad as introduced, and would allow anyone to begin building a chicken house without a permit — and therefore largely without scrutiny from state government.

YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE.

But the final version of the bill was more narrow, and merely gave the department the ability to let someone begin construction during a permit lapse, earning it strong support from lawmakers.

The Delmarva Chicken Association estimates that the permitting delay stalled about $30 million in “business investment by builders, realtors, lenders, equipment manufacturers and farmers to build modern chicken houses to replace older houses coming out of service,” according to a statement from Holly Porter, the executive director of the Delmarva Chicken Association, an advocacy group for poultry growers.

Supporters argue that it is still important for Moore to approve the legislation, since it would apply any time the general permit expires for animal feeding operations.

Enacting the bill would “ensure a permit delay by MDE won’t ever again impose a de facto moratorium on chicken-farm investment,” Porter said.

“We’re confident that the legislation will be signed into law, giving chicken growers reassurance that state leaders really do value their contributions to Maryland’s $5.5 billion chicken economy – and want them to be able to grow and thrive,” Porter said.

But environmental group ShoreRivers wonders if it is still necessary for Moore to sign the bill.

“It is unfortunate that the state would seek to change the rules for a single industry due to an agency failure, especially since that change is no longer necessary now that the permit has been issued,” said Matt Pluta, the director of riverkeeper programs at the organization, who also serves as the Choptank Riverkeeper.

ShoreRivers was among the environmental groups pushing for more accountability measures for MDE to be added to the bill, to ensure the agency does not allow major permits to expire before updated permit conditions are issued.

“We’re encouraged to see the Maryland Department of Environment move forward with issuing an updated permit and look forward to reviewing it more closely,” Pluta wrote. “We also hope the department maintains a consistent schedule for review and reissuance moving forward, so this kind of delay does not occur again.”

When major industry permits expire, MDE will frequently extend the old permit so that the industry can keep operating. But in this instance a wrinkle added to state law in 2019 prevented new construction during extension periods.
